rendered.problem_statement: The question asks about Rented Bike Count. The observational unit is one hourly observation, and the intended population is hourly rental demand in Seoul over one year. The estimand is the model-implied association.
rendered.data_audit: The analysis table holds 2,000 rows. The design card names Date_Hour as a time index, so rows are ordered in time.
rendered.method_decision: Selected method: negative binomial. The outcome, Rented Bike Count, is a non-negative integer count of hourly rentals with {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.n_unique}} distinct values, no missingness ({{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.pct_missing}}) and no structural zeros ({{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.n_zeros}}), so a count regression on the log scale is the natural fit for the stated objective. A Poisson model imposes variance = mean, but the summaries strongly imply severe overdispersion: the mean is {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.mean}} while the range spans {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.min}} to {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.max}}, a spread far wider than Poisson variability at that mean. The negative binomial adds a dispersion parameter and therefore gives calibrated standard errors and tests for the predictor effects. With Temperature as the focal predictor (continuous, 249 unique values from -17.8 to 8.7) and optional adjustment for Hour, Humidity, Holiday and Rainfall, sample size is ample: 2,000 complete rows of 2,000. Two caveats to report rather than reasons to switch methods: Seasons has only 1 level in this extract so it cannot enter the model, and Rainfall is almost degenerate with 98.2 zeros (1,964 of 2,000), so it is better treated as a binary any-rain indicator or dropped. Also, these are consecutive hourly observations ordered by Date_Hour (2,000 unique timestamps), so residuals will be serially correlated; coefficients remain interpretable as associations but inference should be regarded as approximate (heteroskedasticity/autocorrelation-robust or clustered-by-day standard errors if available), and results generalize only to Seoul winter hours. Poisson was rejected because Equidispersion is implausible here: with mean {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.mean}} and values ranging from {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.min}} to {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.max}}, the conditional variance will greatly exceed the mean, producing understated standard errors and anti-conservative p-values. Poisson is the nested null for the dispersion parameter, not the preferred model.. Ols was rejected because Treats a bounded, right-skewed count as continuous and unbounded; it can predict negative rentals and yields heteroskedastic residuals given the mean/range shown. A log-link count model is more faithful to the data-generating process.. Pearson was rejected because Only quantifies a single bivariate linear association and cannot adjust for Hour, Humidity, Holiday or Rainfall, so it cannot 'explain variation' in the multivariable sense the question asks about.. Spearman was rejected because Monotone rank association for one predictor at a time; no covariate adjustment, no interpretable rate ratios, and it discards the count metric of the outcome.. One Way Anova was rejected because Requires a categorical grouping factor and a roughly normal, equal-variance outcome; the focal predictor Temperature is continuous, and Seasons has only 1 level so no multi-group contrast exists.. Kruskal Wallis was rejected because Also needs three or more groups and provides no adjusted effect estimates for a count outcome with several continuous predictors.. Welch T was rejected because A two-group mean comparison (e.g. Holiday vs No Holiday) would answer a much narrower question and ignore Temperature and the other context variables.. Logistic was rejected because The outcome is a count, not a binary event; dichotomizing it would discard information and invent an arbitrary threshold..

rendered.problem_statement: The question is whether contact method (cellular vs. telephone) is associated with term-deposit subscription outcome (yes vs. no) among clients contacted in the marketing campaign. Both variables are categorical and binary, so the target estimand is an association in a two-way contingency table of 2 rows by 2 columns, with no claim of causal effect since the design card records that assignment was not randomised. The unit of observation and sampling is the client contact, and the intended population is clients contacted in the campaign.
rendered.data_audit: The dataset holds 4,000 rows and 2 columns, of which 4,000 rows are complete. Missingness is nil in both fields: contact has 0 missing (0 percent) and y has 0 missing (0 percent). Each variable is binary, with 2 and 2 levels respectively. The audit flags 3,996 duplicate rows and 2 repeated-identifier candidates with max repeats of 3,675 and 3,357 and unique ratios of 5.00e-04 and 5.00e-04; these are an artefact of a two-column dataset in which only the two categorical variables are present, so identical rows are expected and are not evidence of repeated measurement on the same client. Consistent with the design card, pairing is false, there is no clustering column, no repeated-measure identifier and no time column (2 and 2 distinct values in the flagged columns are simply the category levels). Design validity for an independent-observations table therefore holds. Note that 'unknown' is used as a level in other campaign fields, but neither analysis variable contains it here.
rendered.method_decision: Candidates within the closed library for two categorical variables are chi_square and fisher_exact. The cross-tabulation is 2x2 with 1 degree of freedom, 0 structural zeros, and a minimum expected count of 52.244; the number of cells with expected count below five is 0 (0 percent). Expected counts are 3,084.24, 590.756, 272.756 and 52.244 on a total of 4,000. Because the large-sample expected-count condition is comfortably satisfied, chi_square is selected; fisher_exact is reserved for sparse tables and would add no accuracy here. Group comparison, correlation and regression methods are not applicable to two nominal binary variables. The reported effect sizes are Cramer's V and the odds ratio, both interpreted as association measures only.
rendered.results: Observed counts are: cellular with 3,078 no and 597 yes; telephone with 279 no and 46 yes, totalling 4,000. The chi-square test of independence gives a statistic of 0.819 on 1 degree of freedom with p = 0.3655. The association effect size is Cramer's V = 0.0143, 95 percent confidence interval 0 to 0.0453 (confidence level 0.95). The odds ratio for subscription comparing the two contact methods is 0.8501, 95 percent confidence interval 0.6148 to 1.175. Post-fit diagnostics confirm the approximation was appropriate: minimum expected count 52.244 with 0 cells below five in the 2 by 2 table. No revision of the method was required.
rendered.interpretation: Magnitude first: the association is negligible. Cramer's V of 0.0143 sits at the very bottom of the possible range, and its upper confidence bound of 0.0453 rules out anything beyond a very weak relationship. The odds ratio of 0.8501 indicates only a slight difference in subscription odds between contact methods, and its interval from 0.6148 to 1.175 spans the value of no association, so the direction is not resolved. Statistically, the evidence against independence is weak: p = 0.3655 with statistic 0.819 on 1 degree of freedom, far from conventional significance at the 0.05 level. With 4,000 contacts the study had reasonable resolution for moderate associations, so the result is best read as evidence of practical equivalence in observed subscription rates across cellular and telephone contact rather than as an inconclusive null. This is an associational statement about the tabulated data only.
rendered.limitations: The design card states the data are observational and not randomised, so no causal interpretation of contact method on subscription is licensed; contact channel may be confounded with unmeasured client characteristics that were excluded from this two-column extract. The telephone stratum is much smaller than the cellular stratum (279 plus 46 versus 3,078 plus 597), which widens the odds-ratio interval and limits precision for that group even though expected counts remain adequate (52.244). Inference generalises only to clients contacted in this campaign, the intended population on the design card. The chi-square test addresses independence in the whole table and does not adjust for covariates; no multivariable model was in scope here. Finally, the flagged duplicate rows (3,996) mean the data cannot be re-checked for hidden within-client repetition using these columns alone, so the independence-of-contacts assumption rests on the design card rather than on the data.

rejected.fisher_exact: Technically eligible, but the exact test is only needed for sparse tables; here the minimum expected count is {{r2.check_contingency.min_expected}} with {{r2.check_contingency.n_cells_expected_lt_5}} sparse cells out of the {{r2.check_contingency.n_rows}}-by-{{r2.check_contingency.n_cols}} table and total {{r2.check_contingency.total_n}}, so the asymptotic test is preferred and the two would agree.
rejected.logistic: Would model subscription on contact method, but the objective is a plain association test between two categorical variables with {{r2.check_contingency.degrees_of_freedom}} degree of freedom and no covariates in the schema ({{r1.inspect_dataset.n_columns}} columns), so a regression adds no information over the contingency test.
rejected.mann_whitney: Requires an ordinal or continuous outcome; the outcome has only {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.y.n_unique}} nominal levels.
rejected.spearman: Correlation of two binary nominal variables with {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.contact.n_unique}} and {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.y.n_unique}} levels reduces to the same table but does not provide the intended association test for nominal data.

rendered.problem_statement: The question asks whether browsing sessions that ended in a purchase differ from sessions that did not, with respect to time spent on product pages. The outcome, ProductRelated_Duration, is a continuous measure of seconds spent on product-related pages; the grouping variable, Revenue, is binary with levels 'no' and 'yes' (2 levels observed). The design card specifies the observational and sampling unit as the browsing session, with no pairing, no repeated-measure identifier, no clustering column and no time ordering, and the source states each session belongs to a different user. This is therefore a two-independent-groups comparison of a continuous outcome, targeting the population of sessions on the retailer's site over one year. Assignment was not randomised, so the target is a descriptive between-group contrast, not a causal effect.
rendered.data_audit:
The table contains 4,000 rows and 2 columns, with 4,000 complete rows. Missingness is nil in both analysis variables: ProductRelated_Duration has 0 missing values (0 percent) and Revenue has 0 (0 percent). The outcome takes 3,409 distinct values over the range 0 to 21,857.05, with mean 1,183.51 and a floor mass of 255 exact zeros (6.375 percent), consistent with sessions that never opened a product page.

The inspector flagged 2 repeated-value candidates, but neither implies dependence: the first is the group label itself (2 unique values, max repeats 3,395), and the second is the outcome column, whose repeats (255 at maximum, unique ratio 0.8522) are driven by the zero floor. The 564 duplicate rows are duplicate value pairs on only two columns, expected in a coarse two-column extract, not evidence of repeated units. With no pairing, no clustering column and one session per user as stated, the independence requirement for the two-group family is satisfied.

Group sizes are markedly unbalanced: 3,395 non-purchase versus 605 purchase sessions, ratio 5.612. Both distributions are strongly right-skewed and heavy-tailed (skew 3.821 and 3.004; kurtosis 23.803 and 14.222), with IQR-rule outliers of 264 (7.776 percent) and 44 (7.273 percent). Shapiro-Wilk rejects normality decisively in both groups (0.6271, p = 2.53e-65; 0.7056, p = 3.37e-31) and Q-Q correlations are low (0.7912, 0.8381). Spread differs: SDs 1,594.95 versus 2,268.27 (ratio 1.422), variances 2,543,862.01 versus 5,145,059.46 (ratio 2.023), with Levene 84.452, p = 6.18e-20 and Brown-Forsythe 51.744, p = 7.51e-13.
rendered.method_decision:
Candidates in the closed library for two independent groups are student_t, welch_t and mann_whitney.

student_t is rejected: it requires an affirmative equal-variance justification, and the evidence points the other way. Variance ratio is 2.023 with both Levene (p = 6.18e-20) and Brown-Forsythe (p = 7.51e-13) rejecting homogeneity, and the design is unbalanced (5.612), the configuration in which the pooled-variance test is least robust because the larger group dominates the pooled estimate.

mann_whitney remains a defensible alternative given the severe skew, and would answer a stochastic-ordering question. It was not selected as primary because it does not estimate a difference in mean time, which is the interpretable quantity for the substantive question about time spent, and because it does not resolve the unequal-spread problem either (its validity for a location shift also leans on similar shapes, which the differing IQRs, 1,174.67 versus 1,935.45, do not support).

Selected: welch_t. Normality of the raw outcome is violated, but the relevant condition is approximate normality of the sampling distribution of the mean difference, and group sizes of 3,395 and 605 are large enough that the Central Limit Theorem carries the finite skew of 3.821 at most; no single point dominates, since outliers are a diffuse 7.776 and 7.273 percent of each group rather than isolated leverage points. Welch's separate-variance denominator and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom directly address the heteroscedasticity and imbalance. No revision was required after fitting.

rendered.interpretation: [PROVENANCE FAILURE: r4.welch_t.effect_size.interpretation]
rendered.limitations: First, the design is observational and non-randomised, so no causal or intervention claim about dwell time and purchasing is supported. Second, the outcome is severely right-skewed with heavy tails (skew up to 3.821, kurtosis 23.803) and has a floor mass of 255 exact zeros; the mean difference is therefore a summary of markedly non-symmetric distributions, and the mean is a less representative location descriptor than the medians reported. Third, groups are unbalanced (5.612) and heteroscedastic (p = 6.18e-20), so precision is limited by the smaller purchase group (n = 605), as reflected in the reduced df of 714.138; the CI relies on large-sample normality of the mean difference rather than on normal raw data. Fourth, the extract holds only 2 columns, so no covariates (traffic source, visitor type, seasonality) could be adjusted for and confounding is unaddressed; 564 duplicate value pairs cannot be distinguished from genuinely coincident sessions with only these columns. Fifth, independence rests on the source's statement that each session belongs to a different user; it is not verifiable from the data, since there is no user identifier and no time column, and any residual within-user or temporal clustering would understate uncertainty. Finally, inference generalises only to sessions on this retailer's site over the observed year.

rejected.student_t: Requires an affirmative equal-variance case, which is absent: variance ratio {{r3.check_group_assumptions.variance_ratio}}, Levene p {{r3.check_group_assumptions.levene_p}}, Brown-Forsythe p {{r3.check_group_assumptions.brown_forsythe_p}}, combined with strong imbalance ({{r2.summarize_groups.group_size_ratio}}), so the pooled variance {{r3.check_group_assumptions.pooled_variance}} would misstate the standard error.
rejected.mann_whitney: A defensible robust fallback given skew {{r2.summarize_groups.max_abs_skew}}, but it tests stochastic ordering and its validity as a location test is compromised when spreads differ so clearly ({{r3.check_group_assumptions.variance_ratio}}, {{r2.summarize_groups.groups.no.iqr}} versus {{r2.summarize_groups.groups.yes.iqr}}); with {{r2.summarize_groups.total_n}} observations Welch answers the mean-difference question directly.
rejected.welch_anova: Designed for three or more groups; here there are only {{r2.summarize_groups.n_groups}} groups, so it reduces to the Welch t test without adding anything.
rejected.kruskal_wallis: Also a multi-group rank test with {{r3.check_group_assumptions.n_groups}} groups present, and it inherits the same rank-based interpretation limits as Mann-Whitney under unequal spread ({{r2.summarize_groups.sd_ratio}}).
rejected.ols: With a single binary predictor it is algebraically the equal-variance t test and would impose the homoscedasticity that Levene p {{r3.check_group_assumptions.levene_p}} contradicts.

rendered.problem_statement: The question asks what explains variation in the number of bikes rented, with the stated objective of modelling a count outcome. The outcome is 'Rented Bike Count' (a non-negative integer per hour), the designated predictor is Temperature, and Hour, Seasons, Holiday, Humidity, Rainfall and Date_Hour are supplied as context. Within the closed method library, the candidate targets are count regression (poisson or negative_binomial) on the hourly rental count, with ols as a fallback continuous model and pearson/spearman as bivariate descriptions. The intended population stated on the design card is hourly rental demand in Seoul over one year.
rendered.data_audit:
The table contains 2,000 rows and 8 columns, with 2,000 complete rows and 0 duplicate rows. Missingness is absent throughout: {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.pct_missing}} for the outcome, 0 for Temperature, 0 for Humidity, 0 for Rainfall, 0 for Hour, 0 for Holiday and 0 for Seasons.

Outcome: an integer count with {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.n_unique}} distinct values, minimum {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.min}}, maximum {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.max}}, mean {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.mean}} and {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.n_zeros}} zeros. The scale of the maximum relative to the mean signals heavy right skew typical of demand counts.

Design facts that dominate the audit:
1. Time order. The design card names Date_Hour as a time column, and Date_Hour has 2,000 unique values across 2,000 rows — one row per consecutive clock hour. Hourly rental demand is a serially dependent process: adjacent hours share weather, day-of-week and demand momentum. The design card records repeated_id_column as null and clustering_column as null, but absence of an ID column does not create independence; the sampling unit is an hour inside a single continuous series, so the effective number of independent observations is far below 2,000.
2. Coverage contradiction. Seasons has 1 level (Winter only), and Temperature ranges from -17.8 to 8.7 with mean -3.009. The extract is therefore a winter window, not the full year named as the intended population.
3. Degenerate and near-degenerate context variables. Seasons cannot enter any model with 1 level. Rainfall is zero in 98.2 percent of rows (1,964 of 2,000) with only 18 distinct values, so any rainfall coefficient would rest on a handful of wet hours. Holiday has 2 levels but is unbalanced, the larger level covering 1,808 rows. Hour is cyclical over 24 values from 0 to 23 and is not a linear predictor.
4. Diagnostics available are limited to the inspection pass: 6 repeated-identifier candidates were flagged, the strongest being Rainfall with unique ratio 0.009 and Holiday with unique ratio 0.001. No fitted model, no conditional dispersion estimate and no residual autocorrelation statistic were produced.
rendered.method_decision:
Candidates enumerated and adjudicated in the protocol order — design validity first.

poisson / negative_binomial: both assume observations are independent conditional on the mean function. The unit is one hour in an unbroken hourly series (2,000 consecutive timestamps), so residuals will be strongly autocorrelated. Neither Poisson nor negative binomial in this library carries an autoregressive term, a lagged outcome, or a cluster-robust/HAC covariance option, so the standard errors and p-values they would report are known in advance to be too small by an unquantified factor. The choice between them is additionally undecidable here: the protocol requires conditional dispersion after fitting, and no fitted dispersion diagnostic exists in the evidence — the marginal spread implied by the gap between mean {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.mean}} and maximum {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.max}} is explicitly not admissible evidence for that decision.

ols: same dependence violation, and it discards the count nature of an outcome bounded below at {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.min}}.

pearson / spearman: correlation between Temperature and the count is descriptively computable, but its inference machinery also assumes independent draws; with serial dependence the test-level evidence is not interpretable, and a bivariate correlation does not answer a multi-predictor 'what explains variation' question.

Group and categorical methods (student_t, welch_t, mann_whitney, one_way_anova, welch_anova, kruskal_wallis, chi_square, fisher_exact): inapplicable — the outcome is a count, not a group contrast, and Seasons is degenerate at 1 level.

Decision: abstain. The library contains no method that respects the time-ordered dependence of the sampling unit, and the one design fact that would license a count regression — exchangeable, independent hourly observations — is contradicted by the design card's own time column. This is a design-validity abstention, not a distributional one; it would not be resolved by transforming the outcome or by switching from Poisson to negative binomial.
rendered.results:
No inferential model was fitted, so no coefficient, rate ratio, dispersion parameter, interval or p-value is reported. The recorded evidence is descriptive only.

Outcome (Rented Bike Count): minimum {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.min}}, mean {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.mean}}, maximum {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.max}}, distinct values {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.n_unique}}, zeros {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.n_zeros}}, missing {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.Rented Bike Count.n_missing}}.

Predictor (Temperature): minimum -17.8, mean -3.009, maximum 8.7, distinct values 249, missing 0.

rendered.interpretation:

One observation per student is therefore assumed, and independence is treated as satisfied. Group sizes are 383 female and 266 male, ratio 1.44, total 649. The Shapiro rejections are driven by mild left skew rather than extreme shape, the Q-Q linearity is high in both groups (0.9663 and 0.9551), the smaller group has 266 observations, and outlier fractions are small; the sampling distribution of the mean difference is therefore well approximated at this sample size. Assumption tests were weighed as evidence, not treated as switches: normality tests reject at n in the hundreds for negligible departures, so group size, spread, skew and Q-Q behaviour were read jointly. Diagnostics after fitting show no revision trigger: the Welch denominator degrees of freedom 547.439 sit close to the pooled value, confirming the variance correction is minor and that no distributional pathology dominates; no revision was made.
rendered.results: Welch's two-sample t-test on 649 students in 2 groups (383 female, 266 male). Group means: 12.253 (sd 3.124) for females and 11.406 (sd 3.321) for males; medians 12 and 11. Estimated mean difference (female minus male) 0.8472 grade points, standard error 0.2587, 0.95 confidence interval 0.339 to 1.355. Test statistic t = 3.275 on 547.439 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0011. Standardised effect size Cohen's d_av = 0.2628, 0.95 confidence interval 0.1057 to 0.4199.

Statistical evidence: the difference is unlikely under the no-difference hypothesis, t = 3.275, p = 0.0011, and the confidence interval excludes zero, so a direction (female advantage) is resolved. Substantively, the gap is small enough that sex is a weak descriptor of an individual student's final grade even though the group-level difference is reliably detected. Because assignment was not randomised, this is an observed association between sex and final grade in this population, not an effect of sex; any number of unmodelled correlates (school, study time, prior failures, background) could account for it.

rendered.problem_statement: The question asked is whether the condition ("before" versus "after") changes the measured value. The outcome is `value`, continuous; the grouping variable is `condition`, with 2 levels; and `subject_id` is declared in the design card as a repeated-measures identifier. The analysis objective is first to establish whether any method in the supported library is valid for this design, and only then to estimate a condition effect. The decision therefore turns on a design question — whether the 200 rows can be treated as independent observations — before any distributional question is worth asking.
rendered.data_audit:
The table has 200 rows and 3 columns, with 200 complete rows and 0 duplicate rows. Missingness is nil throughout: `value` 0 percent missing (0 cells), `condition` 0 percent (0 cells), `subject_id` 0 percent (0 cells). The outcome is genuinely continuous: 200 distinct values across 200 rows, range -3.678 to 5.096, mean 0.6154, with 0 zeros (0 percent).

The decisive audit finding concerns structure. The inspector flagged 2 repeated-identifier candidates. `condition` itself repeats (2 unique levels, max repeats 100, unique ratio 0.01) — that is simply the group variable. The substantive one is `subject_id`: 50 unique subjects, mean repeats 4 and maximum repeats 4 per subject, unique ratio 0.25. So the 200 rows are not 200 independent measurements; they are repeated measurements nested within 50 subjects. There is no time column, and the design card sets `pairing` to false, so the rows cannot be reduced to one clean matched pair per subject either: each subject contributes several observations, and with mean repeats 4 across 2 conditions the likely layout is multiple replicate measurements per subject per condition. The effective sample size for a condition contrast is on the order of 50, not 200.
rendered.method_decision:
Candidates enumerated for a two-level grouping variable with a continuous outcome: student_t, welch_t, mann_whitney, and — as a regression framing — ols with condition as predictor.

All four share the same requirement: observations must be independent conditional on the group. That requirement fails here. Each of the 50 subjects appears up to 4 times, so measurements within a subject are correlated by construction. Treating them as independent would inflate the degrees of freedom roughly fourfold and shrink standard errors accordingly, producing anti-conservative p-values and confidence intervals with far below nominal coverage. This is a design-validity failure, and by the protocol it precedes and overrides any distributional assessment — no amount of normality or equal-variance evidence can repair it. Welch does not help: it corrects for unequal variances, not for within-unit dependence. Mann-Whitney does not help either: the rank-sum null also assumes independent draws, and its stochastic-ordering statement is equally distorted by clustering.

The two repairs that would work are outside the closed library. One is a paired/within-subject analysis, which requires a defensible one-value-per-subject-per-condition reduction; the design card explicitly sets `pairing` to false and provides no time ordering, so I cannot assert that the before and after replicates align into pairs, and inventing an aggregation rule would be an unrecorded modelling decision on a material design fact. The other is a mixed-effects model or a cluster-robust / GEE specification with a subject random effect, and neither mixed models nor cluster-robust variance estimation is in the supported set; plain ols offers no subject-level error component.

Decision: abstain. No method in the supported library — student_t, welch_t, mann_whitney, one_way_anova, welch_anova, kruskal_wallis, chi_square, fisher_exact, pearson, spearman, ols, logistic, poisson, negative_binomial — provides a valid test of the condition effect for a design with 4 repeated measurements per subject across 50 subjects. No diagnostic on the outcome distribution could change this decision, so none was requested.
rendered.results:
No inferential statistic is reported, because no supported method was executed. Reporting a t statistic, a rank-sum statistic or a p-value here would attach a false precision to a design that does not support it.

rendered.problem_statement: The question asks whether temperature (predictor) is related to the hourly measure recorded in the `value` column (outcome), over a monitored period. The design card describes the observational and sampling unit as an hourly observation, with `hour_index` designated as a time column and no randomised assignment, so any admissible conclusion would be associational rather than causal. Framed within the closed method library, the candidate framings are: a bivariate association between two continuous variables (pearson or spearman), or a regression of `value` on `temperature` (ols). The prior question that must be settled first is whether the design supplies independent observations, because dependence induced by time ordering invalidates every one of those candidates regardless of how well-behaved the marginal distributions are.

The dataset contains 200 rows and 3 columns, with 200 complete rows and 0 duplicate rows. Missingness is absent in all three columns: 0, 0 and 0 missing entries respectively, i.e. 0 and 0 percent missing for predictor and outcome.

The decisive structural fact is the time index. `hour_index` is reported as monotonic, runs from 0 to 199 with mean 99.5, and has 200 unique values across 200 rows. That is a single, gap-free, strictly ordered hourly series: one observation per hour, no replication at any hour. The inspection also found 0 repeated-identifier candidates, confirming that the dependence here is not nesting or pairing but serial ordering in time.

Both analysis variables are continuous with fully distinct values: `temperature` spans 10.225 to 24.675 with mean 17.007 and 200 unique values; `value` spans 3.517 to 42.33 with mean 22.385 and 200 unique values. `value` is strictly positive (0 zeros, 0 percent) and non-integer, so the count-model branch (poisson, negative_binomial) is out of scope on variable type alone. Temperature likewise contains 0 zeros and is not monotonic in time.
rendered.method_decision:
Candidates enumerated and adjudicated:

- poisson / negative_binomial: rejected on variable type. The outcome is continuous and non-integer with 200 distinct values, so no count model applies.
- logistic: rejected; the outcome is not binary.
- Group-comparison methods (student_t, welch_t, mann_whitney, one_way_anova, welch_anova, kruskal_wallis) and categorical methods (chi_square, fisher_exact): rejected; there is no grouping factor, and dichotomising a continuous predictor to manufacture one would discard information and still not repair the dependence problem.
- pearson, spearman, ols: these are the only framings that match the variable roles, and all three are invalidated by the same design fact. Each requires observations that are independent conditional on the model. What we have is one hourly time series of length 200 with a strictly monotonic index over 200 consecutive hours. Ambient temperature over consecutive hours is, by construction of the measurement scheme, strongly autocorrelated, and an environmental hourly outcome will typically be autocorrelated as well. Under such joint serial dependence the nominal standard errors and p-values of pearson, spearman and ols are anti-conservative by an unknown factor, and a shared trend or shared diurnal cycle in the two series can generate a large apparent association with no contemporaneous relationship at all. The effective sample size is not the row count, and nothing in the supported library estimates it.

The closed library contains no method that accommodates serial correlation: there is no autocorrelation-robust standard error, no lagged or differenced specification, no time-series or GLS option, and no way to include `hour_index` as a dependence structure rather than as an ordinary covariate. Following the principle that design validity precedes distribution checks, and that a design fact which invalidates all in-scope methods forces abstention, the decision is to abstain. No correlation coefficient or regression fit was computed, because reporting one would attach a misleadingly precise inferential statement to a design that cannot support it.

Statistical evidence: the departure from independence is unlikely under the independence model, chi-square 13.454 on 2 degrees of freedom, p equal to 0.0012, and the effect-size interval excludes the null value at its lower bound of 0.073. The conclusion is an association between the two classifications among these 420 enquiries; because the design card records no randomisation, this is not evidence that changing acquisition channel would change outcomes, and the result speaks to distributional differences between channels rather than to the risk faced by any individual enquiry.
rendered.limitations: First, the design is observational and not randomised, so any channel-outcome difference may reflect the composition of enquiries arriving through each channel rather than an effect of the channel itself; unmeasured confounders cannot be addressed with the two columns available. Second, the analysis is restricted to two variables (2 columns present), so no adjustment for enquiry characteristics is possible and the test answers only the marginal independence question. Third, the omnibus chi-square on 2 degrees of freedom identifies that the outcome distribution differs across channels but does not by itself provide inference for any single cell; the cell-level comparisons quoted above are descriptive. Fourth, generalisation is limited to the intended population of inbound enquiries; the sampling frame and any selection into the recorded set are not documented, and known missingness was not specified, though observed missingness is 0 and 0 percent. Fifth, exact conditional inference was not available for this layout because the table is not two-by-two; this is not a concern here given the minimum expected count of 61.905 and 0 sparse cells, but it would matter if the analysis were repeated on a smaller subset.

rejected.fisher_exact: Table is not two-by-two ({{r2.check_contingency.n_rows}} by {{r2.check_contingency.n_cols}}, df {{r2.check_contingency.degrees_of_freedom}}) and no sparsity justifies an exact test: minimum expected count is {{r2.check_contingency.min_expected}} with {{r2.check_contingency.n_cells_expected_lt_5}} cells under five.

rejected.kruskal_wallis: Requires a continuous or ordinal response; enquiry_outcome is nominal with {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.enquiry_outcome.n_unique}} unordered levels, so rank-based stochastic ordering is undefined.
rejected.spearman: Needs at least ordinal ordering in both variables; channel is unordered binary ({{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.channel.n_unique}} levels) and enquiry_outcome is nominal, so a monotone-association coefficient is not interpretable.
rejected.poisson: Data are supplied as raw enquiry rows ({{r1.inspect_dataset.n_rows}}) with {{r1.inspect_dataset.n_columns}} categorical columns rather than a count outcome; a log-linear count model is unnecessary when the equivalent chi-square test answers the independence question directly.

rendered.problem_statement: The question is whether adverse event status is associated with site among inbound enquiries. Both variables are categorical: site takes 2 levels and adverse_event takes 2 levels, so the target is a test of association in a cross-classification of two nominal variables. The estimand is an association (contingency) measure for the enquiry population, not an individual risk and not a causal effect. Because the design card records no randomised assignment, the analysis is descriptive/associational only.
rendered.data_audit: The dataset holds 26 rows and 2 columns, of which 26 rows are complete. Missingness is nil in both variables: site has 0 missing (0 percent) and adverse_event has 0 missing (0 percent). Design validity first: the observational and sampling unit are both the enquiry, pairing is false, and there is no repeated-id column, no clustering column and no time column. The audit flagged 2 repeated-id candidates, but these are simply the two analysis variables themselves (max repeats 16 and 14, unique ratios 0.0769 and 0.0769), which is expected for two binary columns and does not indicate repeated measurement. Likewise the 22 duplicate rows are an unavoidable consequence of only four possible level combinations across the observed rows, not evidence of duplicated records. Observations are therefore treated as independent enquiries. The cross-tabulation is 2 by 2 with total 26, cells 6, 4, 8, 8, and 0 structural zeros.
rendered.method_decision: Candidates for two categorical variables in the closed library are chi_square and fisher_exact. The deciding diagnostic is the expected-count profile: expected cells are 5.385, 4.615, 8.615, 7.385, with minimum expected 4.615 and 1 cell (25 percent) below five on 1 degree of freedom. The chi-square large-sample approximation is therefore not adequate, so chi_square was ruled out and Fisher's exact test was selected; it conditions on the observed margins and requires no asymptotic approximation. Abstention was not required because the design is a single cross-section of independent units with no dependence structure to violate the test's assumptions.
rendered.results: Fisher's exact test on the 2 by 2 table (cells 6, 4, 8, 8; total 26) gives an odds ratio of 1.5 with a 0.95 confidence interval from 0.3028 to 7.432, and p = 0.7015. The recorded effect size agrees: 1.5 with interval 0.3028 to 7.432 at confidence level 0.95, graded small. No model diagnostics are applicable, since the exact conditional test has no fitted-model assumptions to check; no revision was needed.
rendered.interpretation: Magnitude first: the estimated odds of adverse_event_1 at site_1 relative to site_2 is 1.5, a small association, but the 0.95 interval spans from 0.3028 to 7.432 — that is, it covers both appreciably lower and appreciably higher odds, so the direction of any association is not resolved by these data. Statistically, p = 0.7015 provides no evidence against the hypothesis of no association between site and adverse event. The conclusion is an absence of detectable association at this sample size (26 enquiries), not evidence that site and adverse event are independent. Because assignment was not randomised, nothing here supports a causal reading: this is an association only, not individual risk or causation.
rendered.limitations: Sample size is the binding constraint: with total 26 and minimum expected count 4.615, precision is very low and the confidence interval for the odds ratio is wide, so only large associations could have been detected. One cell had an expected count under five, which is why the asymptotic chi-square test was excluded. The analysis is unadjusted — no covariates were in scope, so any association or lack of one could reflect composition differences between sites. The design is observational and cross-sectional with no time column, so temporal ordering of exposure and outcome cannot be established. Inference generalises only to inbound enquiries as sampled; both variables were binary as recorded, so no finer level structure within site or adverse event could be examined.

rejected.chi_square: Asymptotic chi-square is unreliable here: minimum expected count is {{r2.check_contingency.min_expected}} with {{r2.check_contingency.n_cells_expected_lt_5}} of the cells ({{r2.check_contingency.pct_cells_expected_lt_5}} percent) below the expected-count guideline at total sample {{r2.check_contingency.total_n}}.
rejected.logistic: A regression model is unnecessary for a plain association question with a single binary predictor, and with only {{r2.check_contingency.total_n}} observations and cells as small as {{r2.check_contingency.observed[0][1]}} the maximum-likelihood estimates would be unstable.

rejected.abstain: No design threat is present: no pairing, no time candidates, and the repeated-id flags reflect only the {{r1.inspect_dataset.repeated_id_candidates[0].n_unique}}-level and {{r1.inspect_dataset.repeated_id_candidates[1].n_unique}}-level analysis variables rather than repeated units.

rendered.problem_statement: The question is whether claim amount differs across customer segments (column `region`, with 3 levels: tier_a, tier_b, tier_c). The analysis objective is a comparison of the distributions of 3 independent groups on a continuous outcome, `claim_amount`, over 144 customer rows. The stakeholder additionally states, and the diagnostics confirm, that the measure is heavily right-skewed. The estimand of interest is therefore whether the segments are stochastically ordered on claim amount — i.e. whether draws from some segments tend to exceed draws from others — rather than a comparison of segment means on the raw scale. No pairwise segment ranking beyond the omnibus test is in scope here, and no adjustment for covariates is requested.
rendered.data_audit:
Design: the observational and sampling unit are both the customer; pairing is false, there is no repeated-measure identifier and no time column, and no clustering column is declared. The automated scan flagged 1 repeated-id candidate, but it is the grouping column `region` itself (3 distinct values, 48 rows each, unique ratio 0.0208); that is the expected footprint of a group label, not evidence of within-unit dependence. Design validity for independent-groups methods is therefore satisfied.

Completeness: 144 complete rows out of 144, 0 duplicate rows, 0 missing outcome values (0 percent) and 0 missing group labels. The outcome is strictly positive with 0 zeros (0 percent), 144 unique values, range 0.2489 to 14.865 and mean 1.894 — a mean well below the maximum, the classic signature of a long upper tail.

Balance and shape: group sizes are exactly equal (48, 48, 48; size ratio 1). Every group is strongly right-skewed: skewness 1.356, 2.61, 3.495, with excess kurtosis 1.908, 9.237 and 15.597. Shapiro-Wilk rejects normality in all groups (1.66e-04, 1.59e-07, 2.60e-09) and Q-Q linearity degrades systematically as skew rises (0.9367, 0.8608, 0.7976). IQR-rule outliers are present in each group (1, 3, 3; 6.25 percent in tier_c), and the group maxima escalate steeply (4.851, 8.923, 14.865).

Spread: standard deviations are 0.9589, 1.497 and 2.311 (sd ratio 2.41); variances 0.9194, 2.242, 5.342 give a variance ratio of 5.81. Levene's test is borderline (0.0515) and the more robust Brown-Forsythe version is not significant (0.1171) — but both tests are themselves distorted by this degree of skew, so the raw variance ratio is the more informative signal: dispersion grows with location, as expected for a heavy-tailed positive measure.
rendered.method_decision:
Candidates within the closed library for 3 independent groups: one_way_anova, welch_anova, kruskal_wallis.

one_way_anova is rejected on two counts. It assumes homoscedasticity, and the observed variance ratio 5.81 across balanced groups provides no affirmative equal-variance justification; the non-significant Brown-Forsythe result (0.1171) is weak evidence of equality rather than evidence for it, given that heavy tails inflate the test's variability. More importantly, its target — a comparison of arithmetic means — is a poor summary here: the group means (1.458, 1.771, 2.454) sit far above the corresponding medians (1.201, 1.379, 1.974) and are driven by a handful of extreme claims.

welch_anova would repair the variance problem but not the distributional one. With maximum absolute skew 3.495 and kurtosis up to 15.597, the Welch statistic remains a function of group means and their standard errors, both of which are dominated by the upper tail; per-group n of 48 is not large enough for the central limit theorem to neutralise skew of this magnitude, and the test would be answering a question about tail-inflated averages that the stakeholder did not ask.

kruskal_wallis is selected. It requires only independence and ordinal-comparable outcomes, both satisfied; it is invariant to the monotone re-scaling that would be needed to symmetrise this outcome; and with perfectly balanced groups (48, 48, 48) and no ties (144 distinct values over 144 rows) the rank statistic is well behaved. The trade-off accepted is the estimand: the test addresses stochastic ordering, not a difference in medians or means. No revision was required after fitting, since rank-based inference has no residual-distribution assumption to violate; the only post-fit check that mattered — that group shapes are not identical, so median language is unsafe — is reflected in the wording below.
rendered.results:
Kruskal-Wallis across 3 segments, total n = 144 with group sizes 48, 48, 48: H = 8.98 on df = 2, p = 0.0112.

Effect size epsilon-squared = 0.0628 (confidence level 0.95); the interval endpoints were not estimable for this statistic and are therefore not reported.

Mean ranks order monotonically across segments: 61.667 (tier_a), 69.271 (tier_b), 86.562 (tier_c). Descriptive location follows the same order — medians 1.201, 1.379, 1.974, with the largest median gap 0.7727. Robust spread measures (MAD 0.7632, 0.9526, 1.18; IQR 1.303, 1.252, 1.606) and quartiles (tier_a 0.742–2.045, tier_b 0.9309–2.183, tier_c 1.153–2.759) show that dispersion widens along with location, confirming a scale shift alongside the location shift.
rendered.interpretation:
Magnitude first: the segments are separated by a modest amount. The largest gap in typical claim amount between segments is 0.7727 on the claim scale, against segment medians of 1.201, 1.379 and 1.974 — a relative difference of roughly the same order as a typical claim itself for the extreme pair, but with heavily overlapping distributions. The rank-based effect size, epsilon-squared = 0.0628, indicates that segment membership accounts for a small-to-moderate share of the variability in claim ranks; most variation in claim amount is within segment, not between.

Statistical evidence: the omnibus test rejects distributional equality at the conventional five-percent level, H = 8.98, df = 2, p = 0.0112. The direction is a clean monotone ordering in mean ranks, 61.667 < 69.271 < 86.562, so tier_c claims tend to exceed tier_b claims, which tend to exceed tier_a claims.

What this does and does not license: the correct reading is stochastic dominance — a randomly chosen tier_c customer is more likely than not to have a larger claim than a randomly chosen tier_a customer. It is not a statement that medians differ by a fixed amount, because the group shapes are not similar: spread scales with location (standard deviations 0.9589, 1.497, 2.311; variance ratio 5.81), so part of the rank separation reflects the heavier upper tail in the higher tiers rather than a pure shift. Because the design is observational and not randomised, these are associations between segment label and claim amount, not effects of segment membership; any characteristic that co-varies with tier could produce the same pattern.
rendered.limitations:
Scope of the estimand: the reported quantity is distributional shift/stochastic ordering. The largest median difference 0.7727 is descriptive context, not the tested parameter, and the unequal group shapes (2.41 sd ratio, skew up to 3.495) mean the equal-shapes condition needed to translate the result into median language does not hold.

No randomisation: assignment to segment was not randomised, so no causal or intervention claim about changing a customer's segment is supported.

Omnibus only: with 3 groups, a significant H identifies that at least some segments differ but does not localise which pair(s). The monotone mean-rank ordering is suggestive but no pairwise test with multiplicity control was performed, and none is reported here.

Interval estimate unavailable: the epsilon-squared confidence bounds were not estimable in this run, so the precision of the effect size 0.0628 is unquantified.

Tail sensitivity: the extreme upper values (14.865 in tier_c against a group median of 1.974; 3 and 3 IQR outliers) have limited leverage on a rank test, which is why it was chosen — but they mean any mean-based restatement of this result would be unstable, and the practical cost implication of these segments depends on the tail, which the rank test deliberately down-weights.

Generalisability and unmodelled structure: inference extends to active customers as sampled; no covariates, exposure or time information were available, so the ordering is unadjusted. Missingness was not declared and none was observed (0 outcome, 0 group), so no missing-data mechanism could be assessed.

rejected.one_way_anova: Requires approximate normality and homogeneous variances; both fail here — Shapiro rejects in all groups ({{r2.summarize_groups.groups.tier_a.shapiro_p}}, {{r2.summarize_groups.groups.tier_b.shapiro_p}}, {{r2.summarize_groups.groups.tier_c.shapiro_p}}) and variances span {{r3.check_group_assumptions.group_variances[0]}} to {{r3.check_group_assumptions.group_variances[2]}} (ratio {{r3.check_group_assumptions.variance_ratio}}), so the pooled-variance F test would be driven by extremes such as {{r2.summarize_groups.groups.tier_c.max}}.
rejected.welch_anova: Welch corrects unequal variance (Levene {{r3.check_group_assumptions.levene_p}}, Brown-Forsythe {{r3.check_group_assumptions.brown_forsythe_p}}) but not the extreme right skew ({{r2.summarize_groups.max_abs_skew}}) and heavy tails ({{r2.summarize_groups.groups.tier_c.kurtosis}}); with only {{r2.summarize_groups.min_group_n}} per group the mean and its standard error remain unstable under such influence.
rejected.mann_whitney: Handles only two samples, whereas the design has {{r2.summarize_groups.n_groups}} independent groups totalling {{r2.summarize_groups.total_n}} observations.

rendered.problem_statement: The question asks whether session duration is systematically higher in one of the two cohorts, with the stated target being an overall distributional shift rather than a comparison of means. The data contain two cohort levels (2 levels, labelled control and treatment) and one continuous outcome, session duration, measured on 117 participants across 2 columns. The estimand of interest is therefore stochastic ordering: how likely a randomly drawn participant from one cohort is to record a longer session than a randomly drawn participant from the other. The design card records the observational and sampling unit as participant, no pairing, no repeated-measure identifier, no time column and no clustering column, so the design is two independent groups of participants drawn from enrolled participants. Assignment is not randomised, so the analysis is a comparison of cohorts as observed, not an estimate of an intervention effect.
rendered.data_audit: Completeness is full: session duration has 0 missing values (0 percent) and cohort has 0 missing (0 percent), with 117 complete rows and 0 duplicate rows. The outcome takes 117 distinct values spanning 0.2122 to 30.155 with mean 2.093; there are 0 zeros (0 percent), so no boundary mass at zero. The single repeated-identifier candidate flagged by the inspector is the cohort column itself (1 candidate, 2 unique values, up to 62 repeats, unique ratio 0.0171); that is the grouping factor, not a participant identifier, and the design card confirms no repeated measurement. Group sizes are 55 and 62 (ratio 1.127, total 117), i.e. near balanced. Both groups are right-skewed and heavy-tailed: skew 1.741 versus 4.839 (maximum absolute skew 4.839), kurtosis 3.019 versus 27.637, Shapiro W 0.8164 (p 8.54e-07) and 0.4927 (p 2.61e-13), Q-Q correlations 0.9015 and 0.6862. IQR-rule outliers number 4 (7.273 percent) and 5 (8.065 percent), with the treatment maximum at 30.155 against a control maximum of 5.134. Spread differs strongly: SDs 1.045 and 4.199 (SD ratio 4.017), variances 1.092 and 17.631 (ratio 16.139), Levene statistic 8.375 (p 0.0046) and Brown-Forsythe statistic 4.771 (p 0.031).
rendered.method_decision: [PROVENANCE FAILURE: r2.summarize_groews.groups.treatment.max]
rendered.results: Mann-Whitney comparison of session duration between cohorts, 55 control and 62 treatment participants (117 total, 2 groups): U statistic 1,091, p-value 8.07e-04, with 0 ties. The probability that a randomly chosen control participant exceeds a randomly chosen treatment participant is 0.3199. The rank-biserial effect size is -0.3601, 95 percent CI -0.5084 to -0.1911 (confidence level 0.95), described as medium. The Hodges-Lehmann shift estimate is -0.5823 at confidence level 0.95. Descriptively, medians are 0.9797 for control and 1.577 for treatment; means are 1.281 and 2.814; SDs 1.045 and 4.199. Quartile ranges reinforce the ordering: control q1 0.59, q3 1.671, IQR 1.081, MAD 0.6367; treatment q1 0.8617, q3 3.23, IQR 2.368, MAD 1.284; minima 0.2122 and 0.3665. Method diagnostics: the rank test requires only independence and comparable measurement, both satisfied by the design card and the complete-case data (117 rows); the tie count of 0 means no tie correction is material, and the near-balanced sizes (1.127) plus minimum group size 55 support the large-sample rank approximation. No revision was needed.
rendered.interpretation: Magnitude first: session duration is shifted upward in the treatment cohort. A randomly selected control participant exceeds a randomly selected treatment participant only about 0.3199 of the time, i.e. the treatment cohort wins the majority of pairwise comparisons; the rank-biserial effect size of -0.3601 (95 percent CI -0.5084 to -0.1911) is a medium-sized separation whose interval excludes no-effect across its whole range, and the Hodges-Lehmann shift of -0.5823 indicates typical treatment durations exceed control durations by roughly that magnitude on the outcome's own scale. The descriptive medians (0.9797 versus 1.577) and quartiles point the same way. Statistical evidence: p 8.07e-04 from U 1,091 with 55 and 62 participants, so the observed ordering is not readily explained by sampling variation. This is a statement about stochastic ordering of the whole distributions, not about medians per se, because the two shapes are not alike: spread and tail weight differ markedly (SD ratio 4.017, skew 4.839 versus 1.741), so part of the shift is expressed as a longer upper tail in the treatment cohort rather than a uniform translation. Because assignment was not randomised, the cohorts differ as observed and the difference cannot be attributed to any cohort-defining intervention.
rendered.limitations: Assignment was not randomised, so cohort membership may be confounded with unmeasured participant characteristics; only cohort and session duration are available (2 columns), so no covariate adjustment is possible within the requested two-group comparison. The two distributions are not shape-comparable (variance ratio 16.139, Levene p 0.0046, Brown-Forsythe p 0.031), so the Hodges-Lehmann value -0.5823 should be read as a shift summary and not as a difference of medians; the probability of superiority 0.3199 and rank-biserial -0.3601 are the defensible effect statements. Heavy tails remain influential in any mean-based framing: 5 IQR outliers in treatment (8.065 percent) including a maximum of 30.155, alongside 4 in control (7.273 percent); these were retained rather than trimmed, which is appropriate for a rank test but means mean comparisons (1.281 versus 2.814) should not be quoted as the headline. Group sizes of 55 and 62 give limited resolution for tail behaviour, so the effect-size interval width from -0.5084 to -0.1911 is the honest precision statement. Inference generalises only to enrolled participants as stated on the design card, and no analysis of subgroups, trends over time or dose-response is in scope since no time column was recorded (1 repeated-identifier candidate was the grouping column itself).

rejected.welch_t: Would handle the unequal variances ({{r3.check_group_assumptions.variance_ratio}}, Levene p {{r3.check_group_assumptions.levene_p}}), but it targets the mean, which the question explicitly rejects, and the mean is dominated by extreme influence points (max {{r2.summarize_groups.groups.treatment.max}} against median {{r2.summarize_groups.groups.treatment.median}}, kurtosis {{r2.summarize_groups.groups.treatment.kurtosis}}).
rejected.student_t: Requires an affirmative equal-variance case, but variances are {{r3.check_group_assumptions.group_variances[0]}} versus {{r3.check_group_assumptions.group_variances[1]}} with sd ratio {{r2.summarize_groups.sd_ratio}} and Brown-Forsythe p {{r3.check_group_assumptions.brown_forsythe_p}}; also a mean-based test on strongly skewed data ({{r2.summarize_groups.max_abs_skew}}).
rejected.kruskal_wallis: Designed for {{r2.summarize_groups.n_groups}} or more groups; with only {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.cohort.n_unique}} cohorts it reduces to the rank test but gives no directional two-sample framing.
rejected.ols: A regression on the raw outcome inherits the same mean-and-normality assumptions violated by skew {{r2.summarize_groups.groups.treatment.skew}} and heteroscedasticity (variance ratio {{r3.check_group_assumptions.variance_ratio}}), and adds no covariates beyond the single group indicator.

rendered.problem_statement: The question is what accounts for variation in the number of incidents recorded per site, and how strongly the single available predictor (predictor_a) is associated with that count. The outcome is a non-negative integer count of events per site; the estimand is therefore a rate — the expected number of incidents per site — and the association is naturally expressed as an incidence-rate ratio per one-unit increase in predictor_a. Each row is one site, sites are the sampling unit, and there is no repeated measurement, pairing, clustering or time ordering declared. The target population is monitored sites. Because assignment was not randomised, the analysis is descriptive/associational: it quantifies how incident rates differ across levels of predictor_a, not what would happen if predictor_a were manipulated.
rendered.data_audit: The dataset has 300 rows and 2 columns, with 300 complete rows and 0 duplicate rows. Missingness is nil for both fields: predictor_a has 0 missing (0 percent) and incidents has 0 missing (0 percent); the fitted model dropped 0 observations and used 300. The outcome is integer-valued, ranging from 0 to 22 with 20 distinct values and mean 2.837; 73 sites (24.333 percent) recorded no incidents. This is a count outcome, consistent with the stated objective. The predictor is continuous, with 300 unique values spanning -2.905 to 2.832 and mean 0.0461; it has 0 zeros, so no exposure/offset ambiguity arises from it. The automated scan flagged 1 repeated-id candidate, but that candidate is the outcome column itself (20 unique levels, up to 73 repeats, unique ratio 0.0667) — an artefact of a low-cardinality count, not evidence of within-unit dependence. No time-column candidates were detected. Design validity therefore holds for a single-level regression: one row per site, independent units, no declared clustering or repeated identifier. No exposure or denominator variable is supplied, so the rate is per site rather than per unit of time or population.
rendered.method_decision: Within the closed library, the design (one count outcome, one continuous predictor, independent units) leaves poisson and negative_binomial as the only admissible candidates; ols is inappropriate for a bounded-below integer outcome with a large zero fraction, logistic requires a binary outcome, and the group-comparison, categorical and correlation families do not match a single continuous predictor with a count response. The choice between Poisson and negative binomial was made from conditional dispersion after fitting, not from the marginal spread. The marginal variance-to-mean ratio is 4.361 (variance 12.371 against mean 2.837), which is suggestive but not decisive on its own since a strong predictor can generate marginal overdispersion in a correctly specified Poisson model. The decisive evidence is the fitted negative-binomial overdispersion parameter, alpha = 0.74, which is statistically distinguishable from zero; a value of that size implies substantial extra-Poisson variation conditional on predictor_a, so Poisson standard errors would be anti-conservative. Negative binomial was therefore selected, reporting incidence-rate ratios with 0.95 confidence intervals. No revision was required after diagnostics.
rendered.results: The negative-binomial model was fitted on 300 sites with 2 estimated mean parameters and 298 residual degrees of freedom (log-likelihood -632.152, AIC 1,268.30). The intercept on the log-rate scale is 0.9015 (SE 0.0634; z = 14.225; p = 6.44e-46; log-scale interval 0.7773 to 1.026), i.e. a baseline rate of 2.463 incidents per site at predictor_a equal to zero, with interval 2.176 to 2.789. For predictor_a the log-rate coefficient is 0.4561 (SE 0.0599; z = 7.61; p = 2.75e-14; log-scale interval 0.3386 to 0.5736), corresponding to an incidence-rate ratio of 1.578 per one-unit increase, 0.95 interval 1.403 to 1.775. Model diagnostics: the estimated overdispersion parameter is 0.74; the Pearson dispersion statistic is 0.9913 and the deviance dispersion 1.106, both close to the value expected under an adequately dispersed fit, indicating the negative-binomial variance function absorbs the extra-Poisson variability. One residual misfit remains: the observed zero fraction is 24.333 percent (73 sites) against 11.173 percent expected under the fitted model, so the excess-zero flag is raised.
rendered.interpretation: Magnitude first: each one-unit increase in predictor_a is associated with a multiplicative increase of 1.578 in the expected number of incidents per site — roughly a half-again higher rate per unit — with a 0.95 interval from 1.403 to 1.775 that excludes unity across its whole range. Across the observed predictor span (-2.905 to 2.832) this compounds into a large difference in expected counts between low- and high-predictor sites, anchored on a baseline of 2.463 incidents per site at a predictor value of zero. The statistical evidence is strong (z = 7.61, p = 2.75e-14). Substantively, predictor_a explains a meaningful share of the variation in incident counts, but not all of it: the fitted overdispersion parameter 0.74 shows appreciable site-to-site heterogeneity in rates remaining after the predictor is accounted for, so unmeasured site characteristics also drive incident counts. Because assignment was not randomised, this is an association among monitored sites and not an estimate of the effect of changing predictor_a; sites differing in predictor_a may differ systematically in other, unrecorded ways.
rendered.limitations: First, the design is observational and non-randomised with a single predictor in the schema, so confounding by unmeasured site characteristics cannot be excluded and no causal reading is warranted. Second, the model still under-predicts sites with no incidents: 24.333 percent observed zeros against 11.173 percent expected, which suggests a structural-zero or reporting mechanism (for example, sites that cannot or do not report) that the negative binomial does not represent; zero-inflated and hurdle models lie outside the supported library, so this residual misfit is reported rather than remedied, and the intercept in particular should be read with that caveat. Third, no exposure, time-at-risk or size denominator is available, so rates are per site and are comparable across sites only if observation windows and site scale are effectively equal; if they are not, part of the residual overdispersion reflects that. Fourth, the predictor enters on a log-linear scale as a single linear term; departures from log-linearity or the influence of the extreme predictor values near -2.905 and 2.832 were not separately quantified here. Fifth, inference generalises only to the intended population of monitored sites, and the 20 distinct outcome values with maximum 22 mean the upper tail rests on few sites.

rejected.poisson: Retained as the fallback but not selected: the outcome tail reaches {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.incidents.max}} while the mean is only {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.incidents.mean}} across {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.incidents.n_unique}} distinct values, with {{r1.inspect_dataset.columns.incidents.pct_zeros}} percent zeros, a spread pattern that equidispersion is very unlikely to reproduce; I will still read the fitted dispersion and revert to Poisson only if it sits near unity.

Selected method: ols with delivery_cost as outcome and predictor_a and predictor_b as simultaneous predictors. This matches a continuous outcome, independent observations, and the multi-predictor conditional-mean estimand. The model was fitted on 260 observations with 0 dropped for missingness, 3 estimated parameters and 257 residual degrees of freedom. Intervals are 95 percent (confidence level 0.95).

Overall fit: R-squared 0.7495, adjusted R-squared 0.7475, residual standard deviation 0.9791, F statistic 384.384 with p 5.71e-78. Information criteria: AIC 729.843, BIC 740.525.

Coefficients (conditional on the other predictor in the model):
- Intercept: estimate 0.4973, standard error 0.0611, t 8.136, p 1.76e-14, 95 percent interval 0.377 to 0.6177.
- predictor_a: estimate 1.576, standard error 0.061, t 25.83, p 2.21e-73, 95 percent interval 1.456 to 1.697.
- predictor_b: estimate -0.6454, standard error 0.0612, t -10.543, p 7.84e-22, 95 percent interval -0.7659 to -0.5248.

Diagnostics after fitting: Breusch–Pagan p 0.139, White p 0.5218, Jarque–Bera p 0.2851, residual skew -0.1984, Durbin–Watson 2.006, max VIF 1, max Cook's distance 0.0475 with 18 flagged points.
rendered.interpretation:
Magnitude first. Both predictors are related to delivery cost, and in opposite directions. A one-unit increase in predictor_a is associated with a change in mean delivery cost of 1.576 units, holding predictor_b fixed, with a plausible range of 1.456 to 1.697. A one-unit increase in predictor_b is associated with a change of -0.6454 units, holding predictor_a fixed, with a plausible range of -0.7659 to -0.5248. On the common scale of these variables the predictor_a association is roughly the larger of the two in absolute size; predictor_b moves cost in the opposite direction. At predictor values of zero the fitted mean cost is 0.4973 (0.377 to 0.6177).

Statistical evidence. Neither interval includes zero and both slopes are far from the conventional threshold: p 2.21e-73 for predictor_a and p 7.84e-22 for predictor_b. The joint test of the two slopes gives F 384.384 with p 5.71e-78. Together the two predictors account for a substantial share of outcome variation, R-squared 0.7495 (adjusted 0.7475), leaving residual spread of 0.9791 — so the model is informative but far from deterministic for any individual observation.

Because max VIF is 1, the two predictors are essentially uncorrelated with each other, so each coefficient is close to its unadjusted association and the two effects can be read independently. The estimands are conditional means: coefficients describe differences in average delivery cost between observations that differ in one predictor while sharing the other, within the sampled units. The design card records no randomised assignment, so these are associations only, not effects of intervening on the predictors.
rendered.limitations: The design was not randomised, so no causal interpretation is licensed; unmeasured determinants of delivery cost that correlate with either predictor would bias these slopes as descriptions of any intervention. Coefficients are conditional on exactly the two predictors included; the library scope covers only the predictors supplied, and any omitted driver of cost is absorbed into the residual spread of 0.9791. Predictor coverage limits interpolation: statements apply within the observed ranges, -2.875 to 2.696 and -2.793 to 3.109, and the intercept sits inside that range only nominally. 18 observations exceeded the routine influence screen; the maximum Cook's distance of 0.0475 indicates none of them drives the fit, but the estimates were not refit with them excluded.
